Exploratory results · not yet validated

Candidate climate refugia from route-level bird trends

Where do species that distribution models expect to lose ground decline the least? A species-voting analysis combining Breeding Bird Survey trends with SDM range-change predictions.

Data BBS route counts, 2010–2025 Trend model iCAR negative-binomial slope, anthro covariate version Scenario RCP 4.5 Scope 469 species × 3,161 routes Prepared 25 September 2026, updated 28 September 2026

SummaryQuestion & dataWhy this designMethodResultsInterpretationLimitationsFor discussionReproducing

Summary

  • Goal. Find routes where a species predicted to lose climate suitability (SDM “contraction”) shows the least decline in observed trends: candidate refugia.
  • Method. Each eligible species runs its own local spatial statistic (Getis-Ord Gi*) on its routes and then votes for the places where it does best. A route’s score is the number of independent species that agree. Capping each species’ influence fixes a failure of our earlier pooled analysis, where one introduced species (Eurasian Collared-Dove) produced about half of the significant hot spots.
  • Almost no route beats chance — but one now does. Under the top1, fractional and cluster rules, no route scores above the level random placement would produce. Under the more permissive top3 rule, one route (Michigan’s 49-5, 5 species voting) exceeds its chance threshold (4) for the first time in this project — see the note in §4.1 for what that does and does not establish.
  • Neighborhoods do cluster. Testing groups of nearby routes, significant high-vote neighborhoods appear under every rule. With the cluster rule, 124 routes qualify, 89 of them (72%) in five Rocky Mountain and Intermountain states (WY, ID, MT, UT, CO). A separate cluster in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula has the top or tied-top route under three of the four rules and the most habitat-diverse set of voting species.
  • Read with care. 80% of the cluster-rule votes are for routes where even the credible lower bound of the trend is still negative, so these are places of relative resilience, not stable or growing populations. About 36% of votes sit at routes where the species was detected in two or fewer years. Results come from one model and one scenario.

Updated 28 September 2026: the species-eligibility ceiling was raised from 150 to 300 contraction-predicted routes (see §3, step 2) after checking the underlying distribution — this added 39 species (163→202 eligible) without re-admitting the very widespread generalists (Mallard, Song Sparrow, Canada Goose, …) the ceiling exists to exclude. The change strengthened, rather than altered, the picture below: same regions, more corroborating species, one route now individually significant under one of the four rules.

1. Question and data

Climate refugia are places where a species persists while conditions elsewhere in its range turn unsuitable. We operationalize this at the level of a single Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) route: for a species that the SDM says should be losing suitability there, is the observed trend better than at the species’ other contraction-predicted routes, and do several different species agree on the same locations?

Inputs
InputWhat it is
Observed trendRoute-level population trend per species from a Bayesian intrinsic-CAR negative-binomial model (log λ = αr + βr·t), fit to BBS counts 2010–2025. Reported as trend = 100(eβ − 1) % per year with a 90% credible interval (trend_lci, trend_uci). This report uses the anthro version, which adds a land-use covariate. Per-route convergence check (R-hat < 1.01, bulk ESS > 400); no rows were dropped.
Predicted range changeClassified-change SDM rasters (Bateman et al. 2020) for RCP 4.5, sampled at each route’s coordinates. Values 1–3 (extirpation, worsening, slightly worsening) are treated as contraction; 4 stable; 5–7 improving or colonization; 0 never suitable.
Scope469 species, 3,161 routes, 12 habitat groups, 259,490 species-by-route trend estimates. Under RCP 4.5, 29,464 of these are contraction-predicted, covering 424 species.

“Trend” is one fitted slope over 16 years, an average compounding rate. It is not a claim about every individual year (see Limitations).

2. Why the analysis takes this form

The species-voting design was reached after three earlier approaches ran into problems. They are summarized here because colleagues will ask about them.

2.1 Credibility, not a fixed magnitude cutoff

The first version flagged a “mismatch” when a contraction-predicted species had a positive observed trend. How many rows qualify depends heavily on the rule, and most of the difference is estimation noise: the median 90% credible interval on a route trend is 10.6 percentage points wide (base model; IQR 8.1–14.2, n = 259,490), and it is about twice as wide for rare species as for abundant ones (14.3 vs 7.4 points in the lowest and highest abundance deciles).

Share of contraction-predicted species–route rows counted as a “mismatch” (base model, RCP 4.5, n = 29,073)
RuleRowsShare
Trend ≥ 0 (any non-negative point estimate)10,59436.4%
Trend ≥ +1.2 %/yr (the annualized PIF Watch List benchmark, applied symmetrically)7,48325.7%
Credible: 90% interval entirely above zero (trend_lci > 0)1,2754.4%

We adopted the credibility criterion because it asks whether the model is confident about a trend, which a magnitude cutoff cannot do. Magnitude thresholds answer a different question (is the change ecologically large?). Every route that passed the credibility test also passed the +1.2%/yr cutoff.

2.2 Pooled hot-spot statistics were dominated by single species

We next ran Getis-Ord Gi* on the pooled mismatch rate and on the mean trend of mismatching species, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) control and a neighborhood-size sensitivity check (k = 5 to 30). Pooling lets one species influence dozens of routes at once. In the anthro RCP 4.5 run, 19 of the 39 species–route pairs behind the 37 FDR-significant “strong increase” hot-spot routes were Eurasian Collared-Dove, an introduced species still colonizing, with Bald Eagle, Sandhill Crane and Trumpeter Swan (recovery stories) also present. Checking raw BBS counts showed 14 of the 39 pairs had two or fewer non-zero years (8 exactly one), so a “credible” route trend can rest on very little local data because the model borrows strength from neighboring routes.

2.3 A single slope is a poor description of individual routes

These findings led to a design in which no single species can dominate and each vote is tied to the species’ own local pattern.

3. Method: species voting

  1. Restrict to contraction-predicted routes. Each species is analyzed only on the routes where the SDM predicts contraction, so a hot spot specifically means “doing better than predicted.” This is done separately for each species.
  2. Check eligibility. A species needs 20–300 contraction-predicted routes. Below 20 there is too little spatial information for a local statistic. Above 300 the species is very widespread (for example Mallard, Song Sparrow, Canada Goose): less relevant for refugia, and with more routes it has more chances to record a vote. The 300 ceiling sits where the eligible-species count flattens out (163 eligible at a ceiling of 150, 202 at 300, only 223 with no ceiling at all), so raising it further mostly just re-admits the handful of most-ubiquitous species the ceiling is meant to exclude. 202 of 424 species qualify.
  3. Run Gi* within each species. Routes are ranked on trend_lci (the credible lower bound), so a route only stands out if the model is confident about its trend. Each route’s neighborhood is itself plus its 8 nearest routes of the same species, with binary weights. The z-scores get Benjamini-Hochberg FDR adjustment (q < 0.05), and a route is “hot” if it is significant and z > 0, meaning the species declines less there and nearby than elsewhere in its contraction range. Species with no hot route cast no vote.
  4. Turn hot routes into votes. Four rules were compared (table below). The cluster rule, our preferred one, groups a species’ hot routes lying within 150 km of each other (single linkage) into one candidate refugium and casts one full vote at each group’s strongest route. A species can vote for several places, but only places far enough apart to count as independent evidence.
  5. Score routes. A route’s score is the sum of vote weights it receives, which equals the number of distinct species voting for it under the top1, top3 and cluster rules.
  6. Test the scores. (a) Per-route permutation test: each voting species’ votes are re-placed at random routes drawn from its own eligible set, keeping the same number and weights of votes; the 95th percentile of the highest score across 499 shuffles is the chance threshold. (b) Neighborhood test: Gi* (k = 8, FDR) is run on the scores themselves across all 2,687 candidate routes, with zero where nobody voted. This detects groups of nearby routes that jointly carry more votes than expected, even if none is individually extreme.
Voting rules compared
RuleWhat each eligible species contributes
top1One full vote, for its single strongest hot route.
top3Full votes for its three strongest hot routes. Caps the count but not the spread, so one local patch can count three times.
fractionalA vote for every hot route, each weighted 1 / (number of hot routes).
clusterOne full vote per group of hot routes within 150 km of each other.

Settings used for every result below: contraction-only routes; rank on trend_lci; k = 8; FDR q = 0.05; eligibility 20–300 routes; cluster distance 150 km; 499 permutations (seed 20260101). Species are analyzed pooled (“all_groups”) and, separately, within each habitat group.

4. Results (anthro model, RCP 4.5)

4.1 Comparing the voting rules

Of 424 contraction-bearing species, 202 are eligible (20–300 contraction-predicted routes) and 155 have at least one FDR-significant hot route, the same 155 under every rule.

Chance threshold = 95th percentile of the highest score under random placement. A route needs a score above it to be individually significant.

What “cleared its own permutation bar” means

Under the top3 rule, route 49-5 (Michigan, score 5: American Bittern, Blackburnian Warbler, Black-throated Green Warbler, Mourning Warbler and Nashville Warbler) scored higher than 95% of 499 simulations in which the same voting species were randomly reassigned to routes from their own eligible sets. In other words, if these five species’ strongest routes had been scattered randomly within each species’ own contraction range rather than landing where the model actually puts them, five of them landing on the same route would happen less than 5% of the time. That is evidence this particular agreement is unlikely to be pure coincidence.

It is not, on its own, evidence of a confirmed refugium: (1) it is one route out of several hundred tested across 4 rules × 9 scopes, with no correction for testing that many combinations; (2) it only appears under top3, the rule built to let several picks from the same species land nearby, so part of why it clears the bar is the rule’s own design, not just the data; (3) two of the five species (American Bittern, Black-throated Green Warbler) still have a negative credible lower bound at this route (see §4.3); and (4) as with every result here, it has not been checked against actual year-by-year counts (§6). We read it as the strongest single data point behind the Michigan cluster, not as a validated finding.

  • One route is now individually significant (above), under the top3 rule only. Nothing is significant under top1, fractional or cluster, in the pooled analysis or in any habitat group.
  • Fractional voting dilutes the signal. Species average 16.9 hot routes each, so most fractional votes are tiny. Its top routes (Iowa, Oregon, Arizona, Illinois) do not match those of any other rule, and we do not recommend it.
  • top3 inflates local patches. It lets one species vote for three routes in the same area, which is why it yields many more “significant” neighborhoods (127 vs 70 under top1) and the one individually significant route above.
  • Cluster keeps the strongest routes from top1 while letting each species contribute to more than one region: species average 3.1 votes (clusters) each.

Regions are bounding boxes drawn around clusters of red points in Figure 3, for description only; the three tables cover 55 of the 124 routes, and the rest lie elsewhere along the same belt and in Oregon, Washington and a few Plains states (state table above). The single highest-scoring route overall, 85-206 (UT, score 4: Evening Grosbeak, Hermit Thrush, Mountain Chickadee, Williamson’s Sapsucker), and 92-77 (WY, score 3), are not in a significant neighborhood — their surroundings did not also score highly enough to pass the neighborhood test, even though these two routes individually rank highest.

4.4 Agreement between rules

  • Route 49-6 (Michigan) is the top route under top1 and top3, and score 3 under cluster (tied with five other routes). It was also the top route in an earlier run with the base model at RCP 4.5 (top1 rule) and with the previous, narrower species-eligibility ceiling.
  • Michigan’s 49-5, the top3-significant route (§4.1), scores only 1 under top1 (it is not any single voting species’ own best route) but reaches 3 under cluster and 5 under top3 — it is specifically a rule that lets several species’ second- and third-best picks stack up that surfaces it.
  • Idaho 33-1 scores 2 under top1 and 3 under cluster; 33-4, its neighbor cluster, only appears once the cluster rule allows multiple votes per species.
  • The Central Rockies signal is mostly a product of allowing multi-region votes, so it depends on that design choice.

5. Interpretation

Rocky Mountain belt. The strongest routes in the Central Rockies are voted for by mountain-forest specialists (Mountain Chickadee, Clark’s Nutcracker, Williamson’s Sapsucker, Western Tanager, Evening Grosbeak), but nearby routes are voted for by grassland and wetland species (Western Meadowlark, Grasshopper Sparrow, Chestnut-collared Longspur, Sora, Northern Harrier). This is a mosaic of guilds rather than one mechanism. High-relief terrain that buffers warming is a plausible common thread, and montane refugia have been identified for other bird communities (for example with SDMs for alpine birds in the European Alps1), but no terrain variable was tested here.

Michigan Upper Peninsula. Eleven species from four habitat groups (boreal, eastern, western-affiliated and wetland) independently pick routes in a small area. This is the closest thing to cross-guild convergence in the results, and its top route holds up across voting rules, across the base trend model in an earlier run, and across both species-eligibility ceilings tested. It is also the only region to produce an individually significant route so far (top3 rule, §4.1). What drives it (habitat extent, low disturbance, microclimate, or the SDM being wrong locally) is not tested.

What the votes mean. A vote says a species declines less at a route and its neighbors than at its other contraction-predicted routes. It does not say the species is stable there: 391 of 488 cluster votes (80%) are for routes with a still-negative credible lower bound (median −3.9%/yr).

6. Limitations

Most important

Under three of the four voting rules, no individual route is statistically distinguishable from chance; under the fourth (top3, the most permissive), exactly one is (§4.1), and that result carries its own caveats. The neighborhood results are supported by a separate test, but everything here should be treated as leads for follow-up, not confirmed refugia.

  • Thin detection histories. Matching the votes to raw BBS data (standard runs, 2010–2025), 36% of cluster votes (172 of 474 matched) and 30% of top1 votes (45 of 151) are at routes where the species was detected in two or fewer years (median 5 for both). The trend model borrows strength from neighboring routes, so a credible estimate can rest on little local evidence. Votes were not screened for this; check route-level counts before acting on a specific route. Four species (Dark-eyed Junco, House Wren, Le Conte’s Sparrow, Northern Goshawk) could not be matched by name and are excluded from these percentages.
  • One slope per route. A log-linear slope cannot represent colonization jumps, boom-and-bust cycles or single high-count years (Figure 2). Trends are best read as a screening measure.
  • Non-climate drivers. Some voted species have well-known non-climate increases: introduced Eurasian Collared-Dove, and recovering Bald Eagle, Sandhill Crane and Trumpeter Swan. Votes were not screened by species.
  • Statistical assumptions. Gi* p-values assume approximate normality, which strains with zero-heavy vote scores. Neighboring tests overlap, so significant routes are correlated, and Benjamini-Hochberg assumes positive dependence. The permutation threshold comes from 499 shuffles, so it is coarse (whole numbers for most rules).
  • Design choices not tuned. Neighborhood size (k = 8), the 150 km cluster distance and the 20–300 route eligibility bounds were set by convention or from the data’s spacing (the ceiling was revisited once, see §3, but not formally optimized). Neighborhood-size sensitivity was tested for the pooled statistics, not for voting.
  • Scope. One trend model (anthro) and one scenario (RCP 4.5) were run in full. The contraction-predicted/expansion-decreasing mismatch analysis was set aside. SDM predictions carry their own uncertainty, and “least decline” is defined relative to each species’ own contraction range.

7. For discussion

  • Is “least decline within a species’ own predicted-contraction range” an acceptable operational definition of a refugium, given that most voted routes are still declining?
  • Should introduced and recovery-driven species be excluded before voting, or reported alongside?
  • Does route 49-5 (top3-significant, §4.1) deserve field follow-up on its own, or is a single route under one of four rules too thin to act on before other checks (below) are done?
  • Priority checks: repeat under RCP 8.5 and the base model; refit candidate routes with a first-difference or GAM-plus-year-effects model from bbsBayes2; add terrain and land-use covariates (elevation, ruggedness, protected areas) to test the Rocky Mountain and Upper Peninsula explanations; decide whether the top3 result should be treated as a hypothesis to test with an independent method rather than reported as a finding.

8. Reproducing this report

5_hotspots.R
Pooled mismatch definitions (credible and threshold modes) and maps.
5b_refugia_hotspot_stats.R
Pooled Gi* with FDR on mismatch rate and strength.
5c_gi_k_sensitivity.R
Neighborhood-size sensitivity (k = 5–30) of the pooled Gi*.
5d_species_voting_hotspots.R
The species-voting analysis in Sections 3–4. Settings: model_tags = "anthro", scenarios = "rcp45", voting_rules = c("top1","top3","fractional","cluster"), rank_cols = "trend_lci", route_scopes = "contraction_only", min_detect_years = 0, require_sdm_skill = FALSE, k_neighbors = 8, fdr_q = 0.05, cluster_distance_km = 150, eligibility 20–300 (min_routes_per_species = 20, max_routes_per_species = 300), n_permutations = 499.
Outputs
output/species_routes_covariates/hotspots/species_voting/ (votes, route scores, neighborhood tables, maps) and …/hotspots/report/ (this report and its figures).
